results.translation: Li Shizhen describes Tong Tuo Mu (the rice paper plant) as having a pith [sui] that is pure white, light, and soft in texture, rendering it suitable for medicinal application. Its nature [xing] is cold [han], its flavour [wei] sweet and bland [gan dan], and it is without toxicity [wu du]. According to the Bencao Gangmu, the pith principally promotes the flow of urine [li xiao bian], unblocks the lactation channels [tong ru mai], clears heat [chu re], resolves toxicity [jie du], and treats abscesses and deep sores [yong ju]. Applied externally to wounds, it is held to arrest bleeding and encourage regeneration of healthy flesh [zhi xue sheng ji].

results.translation: Eucommia bark [Du Zhong], as described by Li Shizhen in the Bencao Gangmu (1596 CE), is classified as sweet in flavor [wei gan] and warm in nature [xing wen], and is considered non-toxic. Li Shizhen records that it principally tonifies the liver and kidney [bu gan shen], strengthens the sinews and bones [qiang jin gu], and calms the fetus [an tai], making it useful in cases of aching and weakness of the lumbar region and knees, flaccidity of the sinews and bones, impotence [yang wei], frequent urination, and restless fetus [tai dong bu an]. The bark is the primary medicinal part used, and its characteristic gutta-percha threads — visible when the bark is broken — were noted by Li Shizhen as a distinguishing feature of the genuine article.

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Eucommia ulmoides Oliv. (Eucommiaceae) — Hardy Rubber Tree; bark (Cortex Eucommiae)

results.translation: Li Shizhen describes the mulberry tree (桑, Sāng; Morus alba) as a plant of exceptional medicinal breadth, with all four of its primary parts — leaf (桑葉, sāngyè), root bark (桑白皮, sāng báipí), fruit (桑椹, sāngshèn), and twig (桑枝, sāngzhī) — entering medicinal use. The mulberry leaf is recorded as cooling [qingre] in nature, capable of dispersing wind-heat [sànfēngrè], clearing lung heat and stopping cough, and brightening the eyes and liver. The root bark [Cortex Mori] is said to drain lung heat, promote urination, and relieve panting and swelling; the fruit nourishes yin [zīyīn], tonifies blood [bǔxuè], and benefits the kidney and liver; while the twig expels wind from the channels and eases joint pain.

entities_mentioned.notes: Bitter, neutral; enters liver meridian. Expels wind-damp [qū fēngshī] and unblocks the channels; used for joint pain and limb numbness. Corresponds to Ramulus Mori.

results.translation: Li Shizhen describes loquat (枇杷, Pí Pá) and particularly its leaf (枇杷葉, Pí Pá Yè) as having the primary actions of harmonizing the stomach [和胃, hé wèi], descending rebellious qi [降逆, jiàng nì], and arresting cough [止咳, zhǐ ké]. The leaf is considered especially effective in cases where stomach qi rises upward contrary to its proper downward course, manifesting as hiccup, nausea, or vomiting, as well as in lung conditions characterized by coughing and wheezing. Li Shizhen notes that the fine hairs on the leaf surface must be carefully removed by brushing before preparation, as they may irritate the throat and aggravate coughing.

results.translation: Li Shizhen describes Shan Zha (hawthorn berry) as sour and sweet in flavor, and slightly warm in nature [qi]. It is principally used to dissolve accumulations of food — particularly from the consumption of meats and fatty foods — disperse stagnant blood [yu xue], and expel tapeworms [tao chong]. Li Shizhen further notes its efficacy in treating abdominal masses [zheng jia], phlegm-fluid retention [tan yin], fullness and distension [pi man], acid regurgitation [tun suan], dysentery [xie li], intestinal wind [chang feng], lumbar pain, hernial disorders [shan qi], postpartum abdominal pain from uterine contraction [chan hou zhen tong], and incomplete discharge of lochia [e lu bu jin].

results.title_inferred: Peach — Kernel and Flower (Prunus persica): Blood-Moving and Intestine-Moistening Properties
results.original_text: 桃 (Táo) — Prunus persica — 桃仁 (táo rén, peach kernel); 桃花 (táo huā, peach blossom). 桃仁，苦、甘，平，無毒。主瘀血、血閉、癥瘕邪氣，殺小蟲。止咳逆上氣，消心下堅，除卒暴擊血，破癥瘕，通月水，止痛。桃花，味苦，平，無毒。主除水氣，利大小便，下三蟲，悅澤人面。
results.translation: The peach (桃, Táo), as recorded by Li Shizhen in the Bencao Gangmu (1596 CE), yields two principal medicinal substances: the kernel (桃仁, táo rén) and the blossom (桃花, táo huā). The peach kernel is described as bitter and sweet in flavor, neutral in nature, and non-toxic; Li Shizhen identifies it as a primary agent for resolving [blood stasis] (瘀血), amenorrhea (血閉), and abdominal masses [zheng-jia] (癥瘕), while also quieting cough with rebellious qi, softening hardness below the heart, dispersing sudden blood trauma, regulating the menses, and expelling intestinal parasites. The peach blossom is likewise bitter and neutral in nature, non-toxic, and is indicated for draining water accumulation, promoting urination and defecation, expelling the three types of intestinal worms, and brightening and润 [润澤, moistening and beautifying] the complexion.

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Prunus persica (L.) Batsch — seed kernel
entities_mentioned.notes: Widely used in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) as an important blood-invigorating and stasis-resolving herb; corresponds to Semen Persicae in pharmacopoeia nomenclature. Contains amygdalin, fatty oils, and enzymes. Still used clinically for dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, and constipation.

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Prunus persica (L.) Batsch — flower
entities_mentioned.notes: Used topically and internally in classical medicine for cosmetic purposes (skin brightening) and as a gentle laxative and anthelmintic. Flos Persicae in pharmacopoeia usage.

results.title_inferred: Mume Plum (Mei) — Fluid Generation, Roundworm Calming, and Antidiarrheal Uses
results.original_text: 梅 (Méi) — 本草綱目，李時珍，1596年。梅生津液，安蛔蟲，止瀉痢。烏梅酸澀，入肝、脾、肺、大腸經。能斂肺澀腸，生津安蛔。治久咳，久瀉，蛔厥腹痛，消渴，瘡毒。 — Prunus mume (Siebold & Zucc.) Siebold & Zucc., Rosaceae.
results.translation: Li Shizhen describes 梅 (Méi), the mume plum (Prunus mume), as a substance of sour and astringent character that enters the Liver, Spleen, Lung, and Large Intestine channels [jīng]. In its processed form as 烏梅 (wūméi, 'black plum' — the smoke-dried, unripe fruit), it is said to astringe the Lung, consolidate the Intestines, generate fluids [jīnyè], and calm roundworms [ān huí chóng]. Li Shizhen recommends it for chronic cough, chronic diarrhea and dysentery, roundworm-induced reversal cold [huí jué — abdominal pain and cold extremities caused by ascariasis], wasting-thirst [xiāokě, corresponding broadly to diabetic-type thirst], and external sores and toxins.

entities_mentioned.name: 梅 / 烏梅 (Méi / Wūméi)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Prunus mume (Siebold & Zucc.) Siebold & Zucc. — Chinese plum or mume plum, family Rosaceae; the dried unripe fruit (Fructus Mume) is the primary medicinal form
entities_mentioned.notes: 烏梅 (wūméi) is the smoke-cured, unripe green fruit and remains an official drug in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia (CP 2020) under Fructus Mume. It is used in the classical formula 烏梅丸 (Wūméi Wán) for ascariasis and chronic diarrhea, consistent with Li Shizhen's indications.

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Ascaris lumbricoides — human roundworm
entities_mentioned.notes: Classical Chinese medicine held that the sour flavor of wūméi 'calms' or 'quiets' roundworms, inhibiting their upward movement and relieving associated abdominal cramping. This reflects an empirical observation that acidic environments may suppress Ascaris motility.

entities_mentioned.name: 消渴 (xiāokě)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Broadly corresponds to diabetes mellitus or severe thirst syndromes; not a single modern disease entity
entities_mentioned.notes: The term xiāokě ('wasting-thirst') in classical texts encompasses conditions marked by excessive thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss, overlapping significantly with type 2 diabetes mellitus, though it is not a direct one-to-one mapping.

preparation.method: The unripe fruit is traditionally harvested in early summer, then smoked or baked at low heat until the flesh blackens, yielding 烏梅 (wūméi). It may be used as a decoction [jiān], pill [wán], or powder [sǎn]. A common classical formula is 烏梅丸, combining wūméi with warming and purgative herbs to treat roundworm reversal. For diarrhea and dysentery, it may be charred (烏梅炭, wūméi tàn) to enhance astringency.
preparation.dosage: Typically 6–12 g per day in decoction; classical sources allow higher doses in pill formulas such as 烏梅丸.

results.original_text: 棗 (Zǎo) — 本草綱目, 李時珍, 1596年。味甘，性平，無毒。補脾和胃，益氣生津，養血安神。主治脾胃虛弱，氣血不足，失眠，心悸，婦人臟躁。Latin: Ziziphus jujuba Mill.
results.translation: Li Shizhen classifies the jujube (棗, Zǎo) as sweet in flavor [甘] and balanced [平] in temperament, and assigns it no toxicity. He states that it tonifies and harmonizes the spleen and stomach [補脾和胃], augments the vital energy [益氣], promotes the generation of bodily fluids [生津], nourishes the blood [養血], and calms the spirit [安神]. Li Shizhen recommends it for conditions arising from deficiency of the spleen and stomach, insufficiency of qi and blood, insomnia, palpitations, and the pattern known in women as 'visceral agitation' [臟躁 — a state of emotional and nervous restlessness].

Both the fresh fruit (鮮棗, xiān zǎo) and dried fruit (大棗, dà zǎo) are used, with the dried form being the standard medicinal preparation. The term 臟躁 (visceral agitation) is a classical diagnostic pattern associated particularly with women, roughly analogous to hysteria or anxiety disorder in modern framing, and jujube features prominently in the classical formula Gan Mai Da Zao Tang (甘麥大棗湯).

results.translation: Li Shizhen classifies Kun Bu (kelp) as salty in flavor and cold in nature [xián, hán]. results.title_inferred: Sargassum / Sea Vegetable (Hai Zao)
results.original_text: 海藻 (Hǎi Zǎo) — 本草綱目, 李時珍, 1596年。類屬: 藻類 (海草)。性味: 苦、鹹、寒。功效: 清熱化痰, 軟堅散結, 利水消腫。主治: 癭瘤、瘰癧、睪丸腫痛、痰飲水腫。[Latin: Sargassum fusiforme (Harv.) Setchell; syn. Hizikia fusiforme]
results.translation: Hai Zao (Sea Vegetable / Sargassum) is described by Li Shizhen as bitter and salty in flavour, and cold in nature [han 寒], acting primarily on the Liver, Stomach, and Kidney channels. Li Shizhen records its chief virtues as clearing heat [qing re 清熱], resolving and dispersing phlegm-congealed nodules [hua tan ruan jian 化痰軟堅], and promoting the downward movement of water to reduce swelling [li shui xiao zhong 利水消腫]. It is held especially efficacious for goitre [ying liu 癭瘤] and scrofulous neck swellings [luo li 瘰癧] caused by the accumulation of phlegm and qi stagnation, as well as for painful swelling of the testes [shan qi 疝氣] and oedema arising from phlegm-fluid retention [tan yin shui zhong 痰飲水腫].

entities_mentioned.name: 海藻 (Hǎi Zǎo)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Sargassum fusiforme (Harv.) Setchell (Sargassaceae); formerly Hizikia fusiforme; a brown marine alga (hijiki seaweed)
entities_mentioned.notes: Li Shizhen distinguished two principal types collected along the Chinese coast: 大葉藻 (large-leaf variety, likely Sargassum pallidum or S. siliquastrum) and 小葉藻 (small-leaf variety, likely S. fusiforme / hijiki). Both were used medicinally with essentially the same indications. The iodine content of Sargassum species provides a modern pharmacological basis for its traditional use in treating iodine-deficiency goitre.

entities_mentioned.name: 癭瘤 (yǐng liú)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Goitre / thyroid enlargement, often iodine-deficiency related
entities_mentioned.notes: A classical Chinese term encompassing neck swellings of thyroid or lymphatic origin; the use of iodine-rich seaweeds such as Sargassum for this condition is one of the earliest documented instances of a rational empirical treatment for goitre in world medicine.

entities_mentioned.name: 瘰癧 (luǒ lì)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Scrofula / cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis
entities_mentioned.notes: A classic TCM term for chronic, indurated lymph-node swellings of the neck, frequently but not exclusively of tuberculous aetiology; treated in the Chinese tradition by 'softening hardness' [ruan jian 軟堅] agents such as Sargassum, Ecklonia (昆布 kūn bù), and oyster shell (牡蠣 mǔ lì).

entities_mentioned.name: 昆布 (Kūn Bù)
entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Ecklonia kurome / Laminaria japonica (kelp)
entities_mentioned.notes: Frequently cited alongside Hai Zao by Li Shizhen as a paired herb with synergistic action for resolving nodules and goitre; often co-prescribed in classical formulae such as Hai Zao Yu Hu Tang (海藻玉壺湯).

results.preparation: Dried Sargassum fronds are rinsed to reduce salt content, then decocted [jian 煎] in water; standard classical dose is 10–15 g per decoction. Li Shizhen notes it should be used with caution alongside Glycyrrhiza (甘草 gān cǎo / liquorice root), which is listed as an incompatible [xiang fan 相反] pairing in classical Chinese pharmacy, though modern clinical practice sometimes disregards this restriction.
